intro: Suzuka's mapped tree gave its name to a cherry cultivar that barely stops flowering. Fudanzakura, the ceaseless cherry, scatters blossoms across its branches nearly year round, pausing mainly in high summer, with a documented spot in a Mie Prefecture temple courtyard going back to the 8th century. One of only 39 cherries Japan has ever named a national natural monument, and free to visit in the temple's walled courtyard.
meta_description: Shiroko Fudan Zakura, Suzuka: type tree of a cherry cultivar that blooms nearly year-round. Free, a national monument since 1923.
question_meta: Suzuka's mapped tree is the Shiroko Fudan Zakura, the type specimen of the Fudanzakura cherry cultivar, documented at this spot since the 8th century.
question_answer: Suzuka's mapped tree is the Shiroko Fudan Zakura, the original type specimen (genbaku) of the Fudanzakura cherry cultivar, one of only 39 cherry trees Japan has ever designated a national natural monument, since 1923. A named cherry has stood at this exact spot since a temple record dated 757 to 765 CE, though the wood growing there today is much younger, roughly 80 years, after repeated fire and storm damage.
question_context: The tree stands in the courtyard of Koyasu Kannon-ji Temple, inside a stone-walled enclosure built in 1832, with a poem monument added in 1868. Fudanzakura means roughly ceaseless cherry: it scatters single five-petaled flowers across its branches almost continuously, pausing mainly in high summer, with documented peaks each March and again in autumn into winter, an unusual double season a Mie University study tied to unusually early September leaf drop. The site's literary record runs from a Nara-period temple mention through 16th-century renga poetry, an Edo-period Noh play, and an illustration in the 1797 guidebook Ise Sangu Meisho Zue. The current trunk is not that old: the main stem died back in 1897, storm damage struck in 1925, a temple fire took it again in 1946, and a 1959 typhoon hit, so the wood standing today is put at roughly 80 years, dating from the fire regrowth. The temple has commissioned periodic arborist checks since 2006 and ran a soil and root restoration from 2011. It is free, open temple ground, two minutes on foot from Tsuzumigaura Station on the Kintetsu Nagoya Line, and the temple still holds a memorial for the tree every 17 March.

trees.story:
Fudanzakura means roughly ceaseless cherry: this tree scatters a few blossoms across its branches almost year round, pausing mainly in high summer, with documented peaks each March and again in autumn into winter. A 1978 Mie University study found why: unusually early leaf drop each September seems to trigger a second, off-season round of flower buds.

It is also the tree an entire named cultivar copies from, the type specimen of Fudanzakura, one of only 39 cherry trees Japan has ever designated a national natural monument, since 1923. Written references to a named cherry here reach back to a temple record from 757 to 765 CE, and it turns up again in 16th-century renga poetry, as the subject of an Edo-period Noh play, and illustrated in a 1797 guidebook to the Ise shrines.

The wood standing today is not that old. This trunk has died back and resprouted repeatedly: in 1897, after storm damage in 1925, a temple fire in 1946, and a typhoon in 1959. The current growth is put at roughly 80 years, dating from that fire. What has survived, unbroken for well over a thousand years, is the spot, the name, and the habit of flowering when nothing else nearby is.

Free, in the walled courtyard of Koyasu Kannon-ji Temple, two minutes on foot from Tsuzumigaura Station. The temple still holds a memorial for it every 17 March.
